title: Reduce tracing overhead with adaptive + tail-based sampling and perf regression fixes
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Summary: Reduce CPU and network/storage overhead caused by pervasive tracing while preserving high-fidelity traces for slow/error cases and representative traffic. Combine lightweight adaptive head-based sampling at the edge with targeted tail-based sampling in the collector to capture rare slow/error traces. Fix several identified performance regressions in the tracer and collector hot paths to lower per-request overhead.

Goals and success metrics:
- Reduce tracing CPU overhead on service side agents by >=35% for 95th percentile services under typical load.
- Reduce trace ingestion storage volume by >=50% while keeping >=99% of error traces and 95% of traces in top 5% latency tail.
- No user-visible increase in request latency (<=1ms median overhead change).
- Validate via canary across 3 high-traffic services and platform internal test harness.

Constraints and context:
- We currently run OpenTelemetry-based SDKs in most services; sampling is configured centrally in the collector but many services use head-based 1% sampling by default which either undercaptures tails or causes high CPU when sampling decisions are complex.
- Storage and ingestion costs have grown with customer usage; full-trace retention is not viable for all traffic.
- Any sampling change must preserve correlation between logs/metrics/traces; we keep traceid as the primary link.

Technical approach (high-level):
1) Adaptive head-based sampling at the service agent: implement a lightweight controller that adjusts sampling rate per service and per route using rolling metrics (QPS, error rate, latency distribution percentiles). The agent keeps a tiny rolling window (exponential decay counters) and periodically receives a desired target sampling budget from the control plane.
2) Tail-based sampling in the collector: configure the OTEL collector with tail-sampling processors that apply retention rules to capture traces meeting error/latency invariants (e.g., status != OK OR duration > 95th percentile for that service). Use a bounded memory reservoir per service to avoid OOM.
3) Probabilistic reservoir with priorities: implement a priority-based reservoir sampler that favors traces with higher error scores or latency while still retaining some probability for representative low-latency traces. This keeps statistical properties for analytics.
4) Move expensive operations off hot path: avoid JSON encoding and disk I/O in the synchronous agent path. Batch and compress spans for export, use a lock-free ring buffer, and use shared memory between exporter threads where available.
5) KV and attribute trimming: trim low-information attributes at the exporter to reduce per-span size based on service-specific attribute allowlist configured via control plane.

Detailed rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (Design & PoC): implement a PoC adaptive sampler in the agent; instrument with debug metrics. (Done: design doc, see links.)
- Phase 1 (Canary): enable adaptive head-based sampling + tail sampling for two internal services (auth, api-gateway) at 10% traffic. Monitor CPU, trace capture rates, and error capture.
- Phase 2 (Expanded canary): add high-throughput worker service; enable reservoir prioritization. Measure storage and query impact on tracing backend.
- Phase 3 (Gradual rollout): roll to 25% of production services, fine-tune thresholds and control-plane budgets.
- Phase 4 (GA): enable by default for all hosted customers with opt-outs and per-customer budgets.

Monitoring, validation and rollback criteria:
- Monitor agent CPU per pod, trace ingress events/s, tail capture rate (errors captured / total errors), and dashboard queries latency.
- Rollback if: agent CPU increases by >5% at 95th percentile, or if error-trace capture drops below 98% for any canaried service, or if end-to-end request latency increases by >2ms median.

Performance regression fixes included in this ticket:
- Reduce span serialization allocations by replacing reflection-heavy encoding path with a precompiled proto/flatbuffer path in our exporter; implement pooled buffers.
- Fix a regression in trace context propagation that caused duplicate span creation under high concurrency (PR ref).
- Batch exporter flush lock contention fix: convert single mutex to per-shard ring buffers.

Testing and benchmarks:
- Synthetic load tests with our stress harness: compare baseline vs adaptive+tail on auth/api-gateway at 1000 RPS for 10m. We expect ~45% CPU reduction on agent and 60% reduction in ingestion events.
- Integration tests: end-to-end test ensuring traceid propagation through gateway->service->db and that trace samples are linkable to logs.
- Nightly regression tests to ensure sampling thresholds don't drift.

Implementation notes and trade-offs:
- Head-based adaptive sampling reduces exporter throughput but may miss late errors that occur after sampling decision; combining with tail-sampling mitigates this.
- Tail-based sampling increases memory pressure on collectors; we mitigate with bounded per-service reservoirs and eviction heuristics.
- Prefer simpler heuristics early (percentile thresholds + error flag) and move to ML-driven budgets later if needed.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- What is the canonical per-service budget API in the control plane (QPS vs daily capture budget)? (Decision pending: we will start with per-minute target QPS.)
- Should we expose sample-rate overrides in Console per-route? (Product/Console decision required.)

Expected artifacts and follow-ups:
- Confluence design doc: Observability: adaptive head + tail sampling (link below).
- PRs: agent sampler, collector config changes, exporter performance fixes.
- Dashboard updates: tracing SLOs, agent CPU, tail-capture rate, storage-volume forecast.

Longer-term: explore using a small ML model to predict trace importance from initial spans to improve early sampling decisions and reduce collector memory.
